nature-gov-070.title: Profit for owners, or duties to society?
nature-gov-070.text: Milton Friedman gave the blunt answer. A firm's purpose, he argued, is to maximize returns to its shareholders, and obeying the law is socially responsible enough. People may spend their own money on causes, he said. But owners should not raise prices to fund social goals unrelated to profit, which he likened to a tax on consumers. This is one side of a long argument. Does a company exist only to earn returns for its owners, or does it also owe duties to society and the environment? The argument is older than Friedman. In the 1930s the legal scholars Berle and Dodd debated it. Should directors be bound by enforceable rules to serve labour, customers and the public as well as shareholders? The other side is {{ref:nature-gov-067}}, backed by {{ref:nature-gov-068}}, which holds that firms owe wider duties. The debate remains unsettled. Some argue better government regulation is the real alternative to voluntary CSR. Others reply that mandated programs distort how resources are allocated. Some studies even find CSR serves managers' interests at shareholders' cost. Economists call that an agency problem: hired managers acting for themselves rather than for the owners they work for.

nature-gov-071.title: The social license to operate: permission no law grants
nature-gov-071.text: A mine can hold every government permit and still be stopped by the people next door. The social license to operate is the ongoing support and approval that local communities and other stakeholders give a company's activities. The term was introduced in 1997, mostly in resource extraction industries such as mining, to describe company-community relations. Communities grant it, not governments. It can take a long time to win but be lost very quickly. Without it, local people may block projects, staff may leave and firms may face ongoing legal challenges. It rests on relationships and trust, so local firms tend to gain it more easily than outsiders. Showing commitment to {{ref:nature-gov-067}} is one way to earn it, by improving a firm's reputation.

nature-gov-092.title: Corporate sustainability: the long game in strategy
nature-gov-092.text: Short-term thinking is described as the main enemy of corporate sustainability. The idea is a business approach that aims to create long-term value for stakeholders by building ethical, social, environmental, cultural and economic concerns into strategy. It is often confused with {{ref:nature-gov-067}}. Scholars say the key difference is time: sustainability asks firms to make trade-offs across time to protect future generations. The idea grew out of sustainable development, as defined by the Brundtland Commission, and John Elkington's 1997 'triple bottom line'. Research usually treats it as three parts: social, environmental and economic. Its most widely accepted test is whether a firm uses {{ref:nature-found-010}} efficiently, keeping vital ecosystem services such as climate regulation and water purification. Firms often state their commitment through Corporate Sustainability Standards, policies meant to meet or beat legal minimums. Whether it can be measured at all remains disputed, because no accepted set of indicators separates sustainable from unsustainable operation.

nature-gov-107.title: The TCFD: telling investors about climate risk
nature-gov-107.text: In December 2015 the G20 and the Financial Stability Board set up a task force chaired by Michael Bloomberg. The Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, or TCFD, writes recommendations that tell investors how companies manage the risks of climate change and how they are governed. It was formed partly in response to the 2015 {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, whose national pledges were criticized for lacking transparent disclosure standards. Its aim is to give investors, lenders and insurers what they need to assess and price climate-related risks and opportunities. Its recommendations cover four areas: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. It is described as the main framework used globally for climate disclosure. Ahead of COP26 in 2021, the UK became the first G20 country to require 1,300 of its largest companies to follow it. At COP26 the IFRS announced the International Sustainability Standards Board, into which the TCFD will converge.

nature-gov-094.title: Creating shared value: profit from solving social problems
nature-gov-094.text: Up to 90% of the ecological footprint in food processing comes from land management outside corporations' control. That gap is one test for creating shared value, a strategy in which a company seeks profit by solving social problems linked to its own operations. The aim is to improve its competitiveness and its communities' conditions at once. Michael Porter and Mark Kramer introduced the idea in a 2006 Harvard Business Review article and expanded it in January 2011. Firms can do it in three ways: reconceiving products and markets, redefining productivity in the value chain, and helping local clusters of businesses develop. Kramer says CSR is about responsibility, while shared value is about creating value. Porter presents it as a win-win, but critics disagree. The Economist called it 'undercooked', and a common complaint is that it plays down the trade-offs businesses must make. Reviewers found little rigorous evidence of its impact, mostly standalone case studies of mixed quality.

nature-gov-082.title: Supply chain sustainability: greening every link
nature-gov-082.text: For many companies, suppliers account for most of their total emissions. Supply chain sustainability means managing the environmental, social and economic effects of goods and services across their whole life. It runs from suppliers to customers and encourages good governance along the way. Traditional supply chain goals were lower costs, just-in-time delivery and faster transport. Rising environmental and social costs and consumer pressure added sustainability as a new measure. Many firms can measure only their own operations, so their true costs are hard to know. Buyers use their purchasing power to set standards for suppliers, treating sustainability like cost, quality and timeliness. Tools include supplier scorecards, {{ref:nature-acct-050}}, surveys and rewards for suppliers that improve. A 2017 study found suppliers farther upstream, away from the end user, had the most to gain financially. After the COVID-19 disruptions, sustainable supply chains proved more resilient. A 2020 Boston Consulting Group survey found 70% of consumers willing to pay a 5% premium for more sustainably made products.

nature-gov-075.title: CSR as misdirection: good deeds as a smokescreen
nature-gov-075.text: The tobacco industry funded research in genetics, viruses and air pollution, drawing attention from the link between smoking and cancer. Critics say companies use social responsibility programs this way, to distract from harmful parts of their business. US firms convicted of bribery got lighter fines if seen to engage in CSR: a 20% rise in corporate giving went with a 40% lower fine. A review of 700 sources found firms engage in CSR mainly for expected financial gain. Supporters still see much of it as genuine responsibility.

nature-gov-078.title: The CSR-consumer paradox: saying green, buying cheap
nature-gov-078.text: Many shoppers say they will buy only from responsible companies. Yet ethical purchases are a small share of household spending. This gap is the CSR-consumer paradox. One explanation is the bystander effect: people act less when others seem not to care. Another is that ethical products cost more but give the buyer little extra in return. A Lisbon study found price, limited access and lack of education held back less engaged shoppers of sustainable fashion.

nature-gov-069.title: Carroll's pyramid: four layers of corporate duty
nature-gov-069.text: Archie Carroll began building his framework after a 1979 article on corporate social performance. It sorts what society expects of business into four responsibilities, often drawn as a pyramid. At the base are economic duties, then legal, then ethical, and at the top philanthropic ones, meaning charitable giving. The pyramid became a standard way to picture {{ref:nature-gov-067}}.

nature-gov-076.title: The resource-based view: CSR as hard-to-copy advantage
nature-gov-076.text: Does CSR pay? One way to judge is to ask whether it gives a firm an advantage rivals cannot copy. Barney (1990) held that lasting advantage needs resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable. Reinhardt (1998) found a CSR-based strategy earns above-normal returns only if competitors cannot imitate it. Waddock and Graves (1997) linked social and financial performance. McWilliams and Siegel (2000) disagreed, saying innovation, not CSR, drove the gains, and argued managers can set CSR spending like any other investment.

nature-gov-073.title: Social accounting: a ledger for society
nature-gov-073.text: Ordinary accounts track money. Social accounting reports the social and environmental effects of a company's economic activity to interest groups and to society at large. It stresses that corporations should be accountable for their effects. There is no single fixed standard. Frameworks include AA1000, based on the {{ref:nature-acct-114}}, the Global Reporting Initiative guidelines and ISO 14000.

nature-gov-074.title: Socially responsible investing: money as a message
nature-gov-074.text: Where investors put their money can reward or punish a company. Socially responsible investing uses that power to encourage behaviour investors consider responsible. What counts as ethical varies. Some religious investors withdraw money from firms that offend their views. Some secular investors divest, selling their holdings, from firms that impose religious views.

nature-gov-072.title: Six ways companies do good
nature-gov-072.text: Companies practise {{ref:nature-gov-067}} through six kinds of activity. They are corporate philanthropy, community volunteering, socially responsible business practices, cause promotion, cause-related marketing and corporate social marketing, which runs behaviour-change campaigns. Philanthropy and volunteering usually have no profit motive. The rest can be cause marketing, which pursues profit and social good together.

nature-gov-060.title: Corporate environmental responsibility: a firm's duty to nature
nature-gov-060.text: Protecting the environment used to be seen as government's job, done through rules and penalties. Now the private sector shares it. Corporate environmental responsibility, or CER, is a company's duty to avoid damaging the natural environment. The term comes from {{ref:nature-gov-067}}, but CER deals strictly with environmental effects inside company strategy, while CSR leans toward social matters. Its main elements are using resources efficiently and limiting activities that would spoil resources for future generations. Government rules drive it, backed by subsidies, tariffs and taxes, along with pressure from media, the public, shareholders and campaign groups. Obstacles include the cost of regulation, uncertain gains, expensive technology and rules that differ between countries. Much is contested. Sources disagree on whether firms must go beyond the law or first make profits for shareholders. It is also unclear which emissions a firm answers for when they are spread across suppliers. Should it answer for past emissions made before the harm was known?

nature-gov-089.title: How business responds to climate change
nature-gov-089.text: Many firms that once denied climate change, including major oil and car companies, changed position as scientific and political consensus grew. Business action on climate change covers everything from cutting a firm's own emissions to trying to influence regulation such as the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. Business helps by investing in new energy technologies and energy efficiency. Firms act to improve their image, cut costs, align with owners, staff, suppliers and customers, and reduce exposure to costs they cannot control. But efficiency often pays off only in the medium to long term, while shareholders want short-term results, so regulation is often needed. By 2007 the Carbon Disclosure Project published emissions data for 2400 of the largest corporations, backed by investors with $41 trillion in assets. Small and medium firms account for around 13% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Physical risks of climate change top the list of concerns for US and EU firms. A 2025 PwC report found 84% of companies keeping or speeding up their climate targets.

nature-gov-104.title: Sustainable sourcing: buying responsibly from the start
nature-gov-104.text: A company is said to be only as sustainable as the start of its supply chain. Sustainable sourcing means getting the materials, products and services a firm needs in a way that is socially and environmentally responsible while still economically sound. Global supply chains and pressure to cut costs have harmed environments and communities, especially in developing nations. They harm nature mainly through resource depletion and pollution, which bring biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and soil degradation. Awareness has grown since the 1990s, when CSR took on environmental duties with Elkington's triple bottom line. Responsible sourcing means obeying ethical rules such as no child labour. Sustainable sourcing goes further and acts to improve conditions. Firms use supplier codes of conduct, supplier selection and assessment, and supplier development. The growing number of standards has raised costs for producers and confused people about their meaning. It relates directly to Sustainable Development Goal 12, responsible consumption and production.

nature-gov-063.title: Social sustainability: caring for workers and neighbors
nature-gov-063.text: A business also answers for the well-being of its employees, customers and community. That is social sustainability. Firms contribute by supporting education, encouraging staff to volunteer and giving to charity. It is often tied to environmental justice, because social fairness and environmental care affect each other.

nature-gov-085.title: Scope 3: the emissions a company does not make itself
nature-gov-085.text: In 2021, 61% of Chevron shareholders backed a resolution asking it to cut emissions, including those it does not make itself. These are Scope 3 emissions: the indirect greenhouse gas emissions in a company's value chain, such as its suppliers' and those from using its products. Scope 1 covers a firm's direct emissions from its own facilities, and Scope 2 the emissions from energy it buys. Scope 3 is especially hard to estimate. In 2020, 81% of S&P 500 companies reported Scope 1 and Scope 2. Rules are catching up. The EU's {{ref:nature-gov-103}} requires large and listed firms to disclose material Scope 3 emissions, starting with 2025 reports on 2024 data. The US SEC's 2024 rule requires Scope 3 reporting if emissions are material or part of corporate targets, though the regulator has signalled it may change this.
